title: Azure Databricks Automation: A 2026 Setup Guide
summary: Azure Databricks automation uses service principals to run scheduled jobs deployed from Git. You'll set up CI/CD pipelines and automate data workflows.
body_markdown:
## Deploy a job from code with bundles


You deploy the same job from code by scaffolding a bundle. Describe the job once in` databricks.yml` with a dev and a prod target, then run validate, deploy and run from the command line or a pipeline.


The click-built job becomes a file a teammate can review.


### Initialise and validate a Databricks bundle


Run` databricks bundle init` and pick the Python or default job template. It writes a` databricks.yml` plus a resources folder holding your job definition. Copy the settings from the job you already built by hand: tasks, cluster, schedule, and the service principal it runs as.


Then run` databricks bundle validate` . It catches a misspelled key or a missing variable before anything touches the workspace. Make this the first habit you ask of the team, because a failed validate costs seconds and a broken deploy costs a morning.


### Deploy to dev and prod targets


Under` targets` , define` dev` and` prod` . Dev uses development mode, which prefixes resource names with the deploying user and pauses schedules, so two people can deploy the same bundle without colliding or firing live runs.


Prod points at the production workspace path and names the service principal as the run-as identity.


From there the loop is two commands:` databricks bundle deploy -t dev` pushes your changes to your own copy, and` databricks bundle run -t dev <job_name>` runs it so you can check the output.


Before prod gets the same deploy with` -t prod` , review has to happen. Nobody edits the prod job in the UI anymore, and that's the habit change the section depends on.


Expect grumbling from anyone used to a quick fix in the console. The answer is that the fix goes through a pull request.


### Run it from a CI pipeline


Have the pipeline deploy, not people. Store the workspace host, the service principal's client ID and its secret as pipeline secrets, and expose them as the` DATABRICKS_HOST` ,` DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID` and` DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET` environment variables.


The CLI picks them up and authenticates as the service principal, so no personal token sits in the pipeline.


In a workable pipeline, validate runs on every pull request and dev deploys on merge. Prod deploys sit behind a manual approval.


Because the principal that deploys is the one that runs the job, permissions are tested on every release instead of discovered at 2 a.m.


You do have another option besides bundles. The Terraform provider suits a platform team that already manages workspaces, networking and catalogs in Terraform and wants jobs in the same state file.


Bundles suit data engineering teams who own their jobs and want a short path from a code change to a deployed run. Many organisations use Terraform for the platform and bundles for the jobs on top.
